processes.description: A trading lead tells the desk which counterparties traders may deal with: a stop on all trades with a named counterparty until further notice, or word that a counterparty is cleared to buy and sell again. Notices from counterparties themselves, such as an energy services company announcing a change effective from a stated time that day, are forwarded to the traders. The notices are brief, sometimes in capitals, and say nothing about scope or when a stop will be lifted.
steps: Credit or a counterparty changes whether trading with that counterparty may continue.
The trading lead or a desk assistant receives the status change or the counterparty's notice.
The notice is sent or forwarded to the traders on the desk.
Traders stop or resume dealing with the named counterparty until a further notice changes it.

automation.approach: Keep one counterparty status list fed by credit, showing each counterparty's trading status, the effective time, the scope and the source of the change, and send desk notices from it in a fixed format so every stop also states when and how it will be reviewed. Deal entry could warn when a trade is booked against a blocked counterparty.
automation.rationale: The notices in the mail are one-line messages such as a stop until further notice with no scope or end condition. A standard notice naming the counterparty, status, effective time, scope and contact would make each message unambiguous for traders the next morning, and the same fields could later feed a status list.

work_estimate.rationale: Beyond the notice itself the hands-on work is small: confirming the status change with credit and making sure the desk's counterparty list or deal entry reflects the stop or reopening, about 5 minutes. A counterparty's own suspension notice may need checking against open deals, up to 15 minutes. Updating a list and flagging trades can be tooled; deciding and confirming status stays with people.

processes.description: For each trading day the risk group, in practice Darron Giron, produces a credit report of counterparty positions and exposure and forwards it to the credit group, mainly Carole Frank, with the report date in the subject. Reports usually go out the same or the next day. After an absence several dated reports were sent together with a note doubting the earlier ones had arrived, and system problems once delayed distribution. Later mail asks that Risk and Credit Aggregation pull the same post IDs so counterparty exposure can be reconciled.
steps: After the day's positions are set, the credit report of counterparty positions and exposure is produced from the risk system.
The report is checked and labelled with its trading date.
The report is forwarded to the credit group with the date in the subject line.
When systems fail or the preparer is out, missed reports are sent later, sometimes several together.
For reconciliation, Risk and Credit Aggregation are asked to pull the same post IDs for counterparty exposure.

stalls.summary: System problems held up distribution of the credit report, and the preparer apologised for the delay.

Reports depend on one preparer: after an absence several dated reports were forwarded together with a note doubting the earlier ones had reached credit, and earlier reports were also resent days after their date.
Counterparty exposure from Risk and from Credit Aggregation has to be reconciled, and a request is made that both pull the same post IDs, which points to the two groups working from different pulls.

automation.approach: Schedule the credit report to run from the risk system once the night's official post ID is set, using the same post IDs Credit Aggregation uses, and send it automatically to a maintained credit distribution list. A daily check flags any business day with no report sent so a backup can run it.
automation.rationale: Every round in the mail is the same dated forward from one person, and the stalls come from system issues and absence. A written procedure for producing, checking and sending the report, including which post IDs to use, lets a backup cover it and keeps Risk and Credit Aggregation on the same figures.

work_estimate.rationale: The quotes show the dated forwards and a reconciliation need, not the preparation, so the minutes are inferred: about 15 to run the report for the day, check it and attach it; 5 when it runs cleanly; 30 when system issues or a post ID reconciliation intervene. Running and distributing is mechanical and can be scheduled; checking and reconciling stays manual.

processes.description: Risk staff, chiefly Darron Giron and Kam Keiser, keep forward curve files and the mapping of curves, locations and post IDs to books. Rounds start when new curves are set up and must be added to downstream tools such as Tagg and Publ Names, when a desk is asked how a location should be mapped, or when the night's official post ID is circulated. A macro queries the official books for a portfolio. For Netco, staff list every curve to be loaded, check their regions for locations mapped to curves no longer set, and modify curve files to load in a new environment and directory.
steps: A new or changed curve, location or book prompts a request from a desk, risk or IT.
Risk sets up the curve and asks for it to be added to downstream tools such as Tagg and Publ Names.
The desk or book owner confirms how the curve or location should be mapped to books.
The mapping is updated and the curve files are prepared and saved in the shared directory for loading.
The official post ID macro is run against the official books and the night's post IDs are circulated.
Lists of new or changed curves and post IDs are forwarded to the groups that load or use them.

stalls.summary: Mapping changes wait on decisions from the desk or book owner: risk asks how an item should be mapped or whether anyone objects, and mappings have to be changed again after other changes.
The nightly official post ID macro is not reliably run: it is described as run most nights and a reminder asks that it be done every night.
Knowledge of the files rests with individuals: a file was obtained from a colleague just before she changed groups, and another region had to be checked by someone else while its owner was out.
New curves are set up in one place and then have to be added separately to other tools, and late additions depend on others agreeing to slip them in.
The move to Netco forced rework: curve files had to be modified for the new environment, regions checked for locations mapped to retired curves and remapped, and files ready by a fixed day.

contradictions.summary: Jason is named as the one running the official post ID macro most nights, yet Darron Giron distributes the macro file and circulates the official and physical post IDs himself in other rounds, leaving unclear who owns the nightly post ID.
The Netco curve lists are said to be saved in one shared path, and later a new directory for the curve files is announced without saying whether the earlier location still applies.

automation.approach: Keep one master mapping table of curve, location, book and post ID, with each curve's status and the downstream tools it must appear in. A change request in a fixed layout records old and new mappings and who approved them; a scheduled job runs the official post ID macro nightly and flags locations mapped to curves no longer set.
automation.rationale: Most rounds are requests to add a curve, change a mapping or list post IDs, and stalls come from unanswered mapping questions, missed nightly runs and files known only to individuals. A standard mapping change layout makes each request complete and traceable, and the same table supports the stale mapping checks the Netco move needed.

work_estimate.rationale: Rounds range from circulating a night's post ID to setting up curves in several tools or remapping a region. Mid 25 minutes covers setting up or checking a curve and its book mapping, adding it to downstream tools and running the post ID macro; 10 for a routine curve file or post ID list; 60 for checking a region for stale mappings or modifying curve files for Netco. Macro runs and stale mapping checks can be tooled; mapping decisions stay manual.
